entries.head:
GOVERNMENT OF INDIA  
MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT  
  
 LOK SABHA 
UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 3366 
ANSWERED ON 07.08.2026  
  
MONITORING OF ONE STOP CENTRES UNDER MISSION SHAKTI  
3366. SMT. DIMPLE YADAV: 
Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:  
(a)  the details of the prescribed infrastructure/minimum service standards for One Stop 
Centres under Mission Shakti including the status of compliance of the Sakhi One Stop 
Centre (SOSC) in Mainpuri, Uttar Pradesh;  
(b)  the details of inspections, monitoring visits/performance assessments conducted at the 
SOSCs in the said region during the last three years;  
(c)  the details of deficiencies, if any, identified during such inspections, monitoring 
visits/performance assessments, along with the action taken thereon, category -wise; 
(d)  the details of proposals received from the Government of Uttar Pradesh for 
strengthening infrastructure, staffing and service delivery of the SOSCs in the said area; 
and 
(e)  the current status thereof and the timeline fixed for addressing the identified 
deficiencies and ensuring full compliance with the operational guidelines of Mission 
Shakti? 
  
ANSWER 
  
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT  
(SHRIMATI SAVITRI THAKUR)  
  
(a):  Under the Mission Shakti Guidelines, One Stop Centre (OSC) provides integrated and 
immediate support and assistance under one roof to women affected by violence and those in 
distress, both in private and public spaces all across the country and are requi red to meet the 
prescribed minimum infrastructure and service standards, including adequate space for 
counselling, temporary shelter, medical and legal support, accessibility for persons with 
disabilities, a dedicated vehicle with scheme branding, trained staff and convergence with the 
Police, Health Department and District Legal Services Authority to provide integrated support 
and assistance to women in distress.  Since inception, i.e. 1st April, 2015 to 30th June, 2026, 
1033 One Stop Centres are administratively approved out of which, 991 One Stop Centres have 
been made operational across the country and over 15.20 lakh women have been assisted in the 
country through these OSCs. 

As on date, 124 One Stop Centres (OSCs) have been made operational in the State of Uttar 
Pradesh and over 3.42 lakh women have been assisted through these OSCs. In Mainpuri district 
of Uttar Pradesh, the One Stop Centre is functioning from a dedicated Government building 
with facilities as per the prescribed standards.  
(b) to (e):   Mission Shakti is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme and implementation of this scheme 
lies with the State Governments and UT Administrations.   As per the Mission Shakti 
guidelines, the Central Government provides financial Assistance to States and UTs. Adequate 
staff and infrastructure support is provided for smooth operationalization of OSCs across the 
country. 
Inspections/Performance Assessments of the OSCs are conducted by various officials of the 
State Government and deficiencies observed during inspections are rectified promptly.  
Further, once in a year, the Programme Approval Board (PAB) monitors with States and UTs 
the progress of activities under the scheme and reviews status of achievement of objectives, 
effective delivery of services to women and children.  Apart from this, officials of the Ministry 
continuously review the scheme through meetings, video conferencing and by making field 
visits to States/UTs from time to time.  
The Ministry has also developed the Mission Shakti Dashboard, which facilitates real -time 
tracking of functioning of the Schemes under the Mission Shakti at the district, State, and 
National levels.  
The Ministry of Women and Child Development alongwith the State Governments and UT 
administrations is continuously working to strengthen the growing demand, visibility and 
timely support to the beneficiaries under the Mission Shakti.

ZERO-DOSE UNDER UNIVERSAL IMMUNISATION PROGRAMME
3367. DR. RAJ KUMAR CHABBEWAL:
Will the Minister of HEALTHAND FAMILYWELFARE be pleased to state:
(a) whether the Government has taken note of global reports indicating that around 13.5
million children worldwide did not receive even a single routine vaccine dose during the latest
reported year and if so, the details thereof;
(b) whether the Government has assessed the number of “zero-dose” children in India during
the last five years, if so, the details thereof, year-wise and State/UT-wise;
(c) the steps taken under the Universal Immunisation Programme (UIP), Mission
Indradhanush and other initiatives to identify and vaccinate zero-dose and under-immunized
children, particularly in urban slums, tribal, remote and migrant populations;
(d) whether the Government has fixed targets and timelines to eliminate zero-dose children
and strengthen routine immunisation coverage in line with global goals; and
(e) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF STATEIN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE
(SMT.ANUPRIYAPATEL)
(a) to (e) The Government of India is providing 11 vaccines against 12 vaccine preventable diseases,
free of cost under the Universal Immunization Program (UIP) in all public health facilities. The Zero-
dose children are infants under one year of age who have not received their first dose of the
Pentavalent vaccine.
 The percentage Full Immunization Coverage (FIC) of India for the Financial Year 2025-26 is
97.9% (source HMIS as on 25th July 2026).
 The Pentavalent 1st dose coverage of the country is 97% (source HMIS as on 25th July 2026)
 The number of zero dose children in India for last 5 years is given in the Annexure.
2. The steps taken under the Universal Immunization Program (UIP) to reduce the number of zero
dose children particularly in urban slums, tribal, remote and migrant populations are placed below:

i. Regular review of the Program by the Central Government through
Immunization Action Group (IAG), National Health Mission (NHM), National Program
Coordination Committee (NPCC) and review by State Task Force on Immunization (STFI),
District Task Force on Immunization (DTFI), and Block Task Force on Immunization (BTFI)
to ensure coordinated and effective implementation.
ii. Zero Dose Implementation Plan 2024 has been rolled out across 143 districts in 11
states with a high burden of unvaccinated children.
iii. Pulse Polio Campaigns are held through National Immunization Days (NIDs) and Sub
-National Immunization Days (SNIDs), India has maintained polio-free status since 2014.
iv. Village Health and Nutrition Days (VHNDs) are organised for immunization and
outreach activities at the community level.
v. Regular IEC (Information, Education, and Communication) campaigns are
undertaken to increase awareness and combat vaccine hesitancy

(a) whether the Government is taking any special measures to promote AYUSH medicine,  
research, education and the cultivation of medicinal plants and to expand AYUSH -based health 
and wellness services in Bihar; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof, district-wise, particularly in Darbhanga District?

THE MINISTER OF STATE (IC) OF THE MINISTRY OF AYUSH

(v) Setting up of upto 10/30/50 bedded Integrated Ayush Hospitals. 
(vi) Supply of essential drugs to Government Ayush Hospitals, Government Dispensaries and 
Government/Government aided Teaching Institutional Ayush Hospitals. 
(vii) Ayush Public Health Programmes. 
(viii) Establishment of new Ayush  colleges in the St ates where availability of Ayush  teaching

(ix) Infrastructural development of Ayush Under-Graduate Institutions and Ayush Post-Graduate

Under NAM, as per the proposal received from State Government of Bihar, through SAAPs,

Ministry of Ayush has set up Central Council for Research in Ayurvedic Sciences

TO BE ANSWERED ON 07TH AUGUST, 2026
WIDESPREAD SLEEP DISORDERS
3369. THIRU DR. S JAGATHRATCHAKAN:
Will the Minister of HEALTHAND FAMILYWELFARE be pleased to state:
(a) whether the Government has examined the growing public-health challenge arising from
widespread sleep disorders, including insomnia, linked to changing lifestyles, workplace stress
and irregular routines in the country, if so, the details thereof;
(b) the measures undertaken by the Government to address sleep- related health concerns
through awareness campaigns, preventive healthcare initiatives and integration of sleep
medicine into primary healthcare systems;
(c) the trends observed concerning the prevalence of sleep disorders and their impact on
physical health, mental well-being, productivity and quality of life; and
(d) whether the Government has assessed the adequacy of existing healthcare infrastructure,
specialist services and diagnostic facilities for addressing sleep-related conditions and the
observations made thereon, if so, the details thereof?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF STATEIN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND
FAMILYWELFARE
(SHRI PRATAPRAOJADHA V)
(a) to (d) The National Mental Health Survey (NMHS), conducted in 2016 by NIMHANS,
provided critical data on mental health prevalence and treatment gaps helping in assessing the
outcome indicators and in shaping future directions of the mental health treatment programmes.
The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) advances mental health research in several
areas, focusing on evidence-based psychosocial interventions and community-based approaches.
To address the burden of mental disorders, the Government of India is implementing the National
Mental Health Programme (NMHP) in the country. The District Mental Health Programme
(DMHP) component of the NMHP has been sanctioned for implementation in 767 districts for
which support is provided to States/UTs through the National Health Mission. Facilities made
available under DMHP at the Community Health Centre(CHC) and Primary Health Centre(PHC)

levels for all including elderly, inter- alia, include outpatient services, assessment, counselling/
psycho-social interventions, continuing care and support to persons with severe mental disorders,
drugs, outreach services, ambulance services etc. In addition to above services there is a
provision of 10 bedded in-patient facility at the District level.
The Government is also taking steps to strengthen mental healthcare services at primary
healthcare level. The Government has upgraded more than 1.8 lakh Sub Health Centres (SHCs)
and Primary Health Centres (PHCs) to Ayushman Arogya Mandirs. Mental health services have
been added in the packages of services under Comprehensive Primary Health Care provided at
these Ayushman Arogya Mandirs. Operational guidelines and training manuals for various cadres
on Mental, Neurological, and Substance Use Disorders (MNS) at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs
have been released under the ambit of Ayushman Bharat. Further, wellness activities are also
promoted at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, these promote mindfulness, relaxation and healthy
lifestyle practices that contribute to better sleep and overall well-being.
Community-based health promotion initiatives such as Fit India and other wellness campaigns
encourage physical activity and healthy living, which are important for maintaining healthy sleep
patterns.
Besides the above, the Government has launched a “National Tele Mental Health Programme”
on 10th October, 2022, to further improve access to quality mental health counselling and care
services in the country. As on 27.07.2026, 36 States/ UTs have set up 53 Tele MANAS Cells.
Tele-MANAS services are available in 20 languages based on language opted by States. More
than 42 lakhs calls have been handled on the helpline number.
Under the National Tele Mental Health Programme (NTMHP), individuals experiencing sleep
disturbances associated with stress, anxiety, depression and other mental health conditions can
access free 24×7 tele-mental health counselling, psychological support, guidance on healthy
sleep practices and sleep hygiene, and referral to appropriate healthcare facilities, whenever
required. Further, as part of routine counselling, Tele-MANAS counsellors promote behavioural
measures to improve sleep, including healthy sleep habits and sleep hygiene.
The Government has also launched Tele-MANAS Mobile Application on the occasion of World
Mental Health Day - October 10, 2024. Tele-MANAS Mobile Application is a comprehensive
Mobile platform that has been developed to provide support for mental health issues ranging
from wellbeing to mental disorders. The Government has also launched the video consultation
facility under Tele-MANAS, as another upgrade to the already existing audio calling facility.

(b) the number of districts in Uttar Pradesh without a functional Trauma Care Centre or where

GOVERNMENT OF INDIA
MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE
DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE
LOK SABHA
UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 3374
ANSWERED ON 7TH AUGUST, 2026
EARLY SCREENING PROGRAMMES FOR NCDS
†3374. SMT. DELKAR KALABEN MOHANBHAI:
SHRI BHUMARE SANDIPANRAO ASARAM:
DR. SHIV AJIBANDAPPAKALGE:
Will the Minister OF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE be pleased to state:
(a) the present status of early screening programmes for diabetes, hypertension and major variants
of cancer under Primary and Secondary healthcare facilities across the country;
(b) the extent to which nutrition education has been institutionalised as part of public health
initiatives including the details thereof, in Maharashtra and the UT of Dadra & Nagar Haveli and
Daman & Diu;
(c) the steps taken by the Government in coordination with other concerned Ministries to tackle air
pollution and ensure access to safe drinking water as a preventive health intervention; and
(d) whether any cost-benefit assessment has been carried out to compare the expenditure on
preventive healthcare with the expenditure on tertiary healthcare and ICU infrastructure, if so, the
findings thereof, along with the action taken by the Government thereon, particularly in
Maharashtra?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF STATEIN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND
FAMILYWELFARE
(SHRI PRATAPRAO JADHA V)
(a) to (d): The Department of Health & Family Welfare, Government of India provides technical
and financial support to the States and Union Territories under the National Programme for
Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases (NP-NCD). Under NP-NCD, 770 District
NCD Clinics, 233 Cardiac Care Units and 6,410 NCD clinics at Community Health Centres have
been set up across the country. In addition, 524 Day Care Cancer Centres (DCCCs) are functional
across the country to ensure cancer care accessibility at district level.
A population-based initiative for prevention, control and screening for common NCDs i.e. diabetes,
hypertension, oral, breast and cervical cancer was rolled out in the country under National Health
Mission (NHM) as a part of Comprehensive Primary Health Care. Under the initiative, persons
more than 30 years of age are targeted for screening. Till July 2026, 42.4 crore have been screened
for hypertension, 42.21 crore for diabetes, 36.11 crore for oral cancer, 16.94 crore for breast
cancer and 9.31 crore for cervical cancer as per the National NCD Portal.

Nutrition education has been institutionalised as an integral component of public health initiatives
under the National Health Mission (NHM) and POSHAN Abhiyaan across the country, including
Maharashtra and the Union Territory of Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu. A lifecycle
approach is adopted to provide nutrition education and counselling through Ayushman Arogya
Mandirs (AAMs), Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Days (VHSNDs), and community-
based platforms. Under POSHAN Abhiyaan, implemented in convergence with the Ministry of
Women & Child Development, behaviour change communication is promoted through the Jan
Andolan approach, supported by nutrition e-learning modules developed by ICMR–National
Institute of Nutrition (NIN). Nutrition education is further strengthened through Rashtriya Bal
Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK), Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (RKSK) and the Eat Right
India initiative. These interventions are implemented uniformly across all States and Union
Territories, including Maharashtra and the Union Territory of Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman
& Diu.
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change has launched the National Clean Air
Programme (NCAP) in 2019 to address issues related to air pollution. Ministry of Jal Shakti in
partnership with States is implementing Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) – Har Ghar Jal to provide
potable water to every rural household of the country through functional tap water connection.
Preventive aspect of NCDs is strengthened under Comprehensive Primary Health Care through
Ayushman Arogya Mandir, by promotion of wellness activities and targeted communication at the
community level across the country including Maharashtra. Further initiatives for increasing
public awareness about NCDs and for promotion of healthy lifestyle includes observation of
National & International Health Days and use of print, electronic and social media for continued
community awareness. In addition, the Fit India Movement promotes regular physical activity and
healthy living, while the Khelo India programme encourages sports and fitness among all age
groups. Various Yoga-related activities are also undertaken by the Ministry of AYUSH to promote
health and wellness.
******

GOVERNMENT OF INDIA
MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE
DEPARTMENTOF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE

UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 3375
TO BE ANSWERED ON 7TH AUGUST, 2026
TRANSPARENCY IN FMGE EXAMINATIONS
†3375. SHRI KULDEEP INDORA:
SHRI ZIA UR REHMAN:
Will the Minister of HEALTHAND FAMILYWELFARE be pleased to state:
(a) whether the Government has received representations and serious complaints from
candidates who appeared in the FMGE held on 28 June, 2026 regarding the inclusion of video-
based questions for the first time, changes in the examination pattern without prior notice, an
extremely lengthy and difficult question paper resulting in a pass percentage of only 12.40
percent, lack of transparency in evaluation, non-publication of the answer key and inadequate
facilities at examination centres during the severe heatwave;
(b) if so, the details thereof along with the action taken by the Government/National Board of
Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS) to examine these grievances and conduct an
inquiry
into these complaints;
(c) whether similar complaints have been received in the last three years in FMGE or other
national medical examinations and if so, the details thereof;
(d) whether the Government is considering to take corrective measures, including the release
of the FMGE June 2026 answer key to ensure fairness in the examination, bringing more
transparency into the examination process and awarding 20 bonus marks to provide appropriate
relief as demanded by the affected candidates; and
(e) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF STATEIN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY
WELFARE
(SMT. ANUPRIYAPATEL)
(a) to (c): The Foreign Medical Graduate Examination (FMGE) is conducted by the National
Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS) in accordance with the provisions of
the Screening Test Regulations for Foreign Medical Graduates (FMGs) seeking provisional or
permanent registration with the National Medical Commission (NMC) or the respective State
Medical Councils (SMCs). The Syllabus for FMGE comprises Subjects/Knowledge Areas as
per the Competency based Undergraduate Curriculum published by NMC for the MBBS

Course.
As informed by NBEMS, video-based questions were included in the official demo test made
available to candidates prior to the FMGE June 2026 examination to familiarize them with
the examination interface and pattern and hence, were notified in advance.
The pass rate in FMGE depends on multiple factors, including the quality of medical
education imparted, individual candidate's level of knowledge and performance in the
examination. The overall pass percentage in FMGE June 2026 is 12.78%. Amongst freshers
(those who have appeared for the first time), the pass percentage is more than 35%.
Moreover, NBEMS conducted audits of the examination centres prior to the conduct of the
FMGE June 2026 to ensure their preparedness and the availability of necessary facilities.
Adequate arrangements were made for candidates at all examination centres including the
provision of additional cooling arrangements such as coolers, wherever warranted by local
weather conditions. Adequate drinking water was also made available to candidates during
both examination shifts at all examination centres.
(d) & (e): The FMGE examination is conducted through a structured question bank
containing a finite pool of validated questions. Clause 9.7 of the FMGE Information Bulletin
specifically provides that the examination is covered under a Non-Disclosure Agreement.
Disclosure of question papers may compromise the integrity, confidentiality and future
conduct of the examination.
Further, FMGE is conducted strictly in accordance with the notified regulations and
prescribed qualifying criteria. Any changes relating to the eligibility criteria, syllabus or
regulatory framework governing FMGs are considered by the NMC from time to time in
accordance with the statutory provisions and stakeholder requirements.

Governments and the concerned High Courts. Under Section 14 of the Scheduled Castes and the 
Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) [PoA] Act, 1989, the States/UTs are responsible for 
establishing Exclusive Special Courts with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of the concerned High 
Court.  
(e): The Department of Social Justice and Empowerment runs a Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) 
for the implementation of the Protection of Civil Rights (PCR) Act, 1955 and the Scheduled Castes 
(SC) and the Scheduled Tribes (ST) (Prevention of Atrocities) {PoA} Act, 1989, under which Central 
Assistance is provided to the States/UTs mainly for five components including Setting up and 
Functioning of Exclusive Special Courts. 
As per the Scheme guidelines , central assistance is provided as per the actual requirement 
proposed by the State/UT Governments towards salary, office expenses etc. However, there is no 
provision for providing central assistance  for procurement of land, construction of buildings and 
judicial infrastructure relating to these courts.  
(f): The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 as amended 
from time to time provides for time bound trial under Section 14(2), witness protection under Section

15 A-Rights of victims and witnesses and Relief and rehabilitation of atrocity victims as per Rule 12 
(4) of the PoA Rules, 1995 and as amended from time to time.

UNSTARRED QUESTION No. 3377
TO BE ANSWERED ON 7TH AUGUST, 2026
STUDENTS APPEARING FOR NEET-UG AND PG
3377. SHRI ANTO ANTONY:
Will the Minister of HEALTHAND FAMILYWELFARE be pleased to state:
(a) the number of students appearing for NEET-UG and NEET-PG separately, since 2015, year-
wise;
(b) the number of medical colleges and total number of MBBS seats since 2015, separately for
Government and private institutions, State/UT-wise and year-wise;
(c) the number of MBBS and post graduate seats per million population, State/UT-wise;
(d) the vacancy position of faculty in AIIMS and other Central Government medical institutions,
Institution-wise and social-category-wise;
(e) whether the Government is aware of reports suggesting a shortage of faculties, delayed
stipend payments and other challenges faced by Government medical colleges in the country, if
so, the details thereof and the action taken thereon; and
(f) the steps taken by the Government to ensure equitable expansion of medical education in
the country?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF STATEIN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY
WELFARE
(SMT. ANUPRIYAPATEL)
(a): The number of students who appeared in NEET-UG and NEET-PG examinations since
2019 are attached as Annexure-I.
(b) & (c): The Government has undertaken significant measures to expand medical education
infrastructure across the country by increasing the number of medical colleges as well as
undergraduate (UG) and postgraduate (PG) medical seats. The number of Medical Colleges
have increased from 387 to 846; UG seats from 51,348 to 1,39,864 and PG seats from 31,185
to 86,360 from 2014 to as on date. The State/UT-wise details of medical colleges and MBBS
seats, including Government and private institutions, as on 30.07.2026 are attached as
Annexure-II.
(d) to (f): Filling up of vacant faculty posts is a continuous process and depends upon various

factors such as the availability of suitable and qualified candidates, reservation roster, and the
location-specific requirements of the Institutes. To facilitate timely recruitment of faculty in
AIIMS, the Government has, inter alia, constituted Standing Selection Committees (SSCs) in
each Institute for selection of faculty, provided for engagement of retired faculty on a
contractual basis up to the age of 70 years, and introduced the Visiting Faculty Scheme to
augment teaching resources.
The National Medical Commission (NMC) has framed Medical Institutions (Qualification of
Faculty) Regulation, 2025 to address the shortage of faculty in Medical Institutions. Further,
Schedule IV of the Compulsory Rotatory Medical Internship (CRMI) Regulations provides
that interns shall be paid stipends as fixed by the appropriate authority applicable to the
concerned institution, University or State. In addition, the NMC, through its Public Notice
dated 12.03.2026, has reiterated the applicable regulatory provisions, penalty framework and
directions of the Hon'ble Court regarding payment of stipends, with instructions to all
Deans/Principals, State Medical Councils and Directorates of Medical Education (DMEs) to
ensure strict compliance.
The Government has implemented following schemes to ensure equitable expansion of
medical education in the country:
 Centrally Sponsored Scheme for establishment of new medical college by upgrading
district/ referral hospital under which 139 new medical colleges are functional out of
157 approved medical colleges.
 Centrally Sponsored Scheme for strengthening/ upgradation of existing State
Government/Central Government Medical Colleges to increase MBBS and PG seats.
 Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY) scheme has a component
related to “Upgradation of Government Medical Colleges by construction of Super
Specialty Blocks/Trauma care centres, etc.” Out of 75 projects, 71 projects are
complete under this component. The other component is for setting up of new AIIMS,
under which 22 AIIMS have been approved.

3379. SHRI LAVU SRI KRISHNA DEVARAYALU:  
  
Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:  
(a)  the details of Anganwadi Centres (AWCs) that have been upgraded into Saksham 
Anganwadi Centres, State-wise and district-wise for Andhra Pradesh; 
(b)  the funds allocated and utilised for the upgradation of these AWCs, State -wise and 
district- wise for Andhra Pradesh;  
(c)  the details of training and support provided to Anganwadi Workers (AWWs) to enhance 
their skills and effectiveness in the upgraded Saksham AWCs; and  
(d)  whether Government has planned or proposed projects for the upgradation of additional 
AWCs, if so, the details thereof, State -wise and district-wise for Andhra Pradesh?  
  
ANSWER 
  
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT  
(SHRIMATI SAVITRI THAKUR)  
  
(a) to (d) Under Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0, two lakh Anganwadi Centres 
(AWCs) located in Government buildings have been sanctioned for upgradation as Saksham 
Anganwadis for delivery of improved nutrition and for Early Childhood Care and Education in 
the 15th Finance Commission cycle. Saksham Anganwadi Centres (AWCs) are provided with 
infrastructure such as LED screens, water filtration system, Poshan Vatika, Early Childhood 
Care and Education (ECCE) material and Building as Learning Aid (BALA) paintings. A to tal

released for upgradation are placed at Annexure I. 
The District wise list of AWCs approved for upgradation to Saksham AWCs in the State of 
Andhra Pradesh is placed at Annexure II. 
The Ministry, through the Poshan Bhi Padhai Bhi (PBPB) initiative under Mission Saksham 
Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0, has adopted a phased implementation strategy for scaling up 
‘Aadharshila’ and ‘Navchetana ’ across all Anganwadi Centres. The major steps undertaken 
include capacity building of State Level Master Trainers (SLMTs) through PBPB Round 1 and 

Round 2 training programmes, cascade training of Anganwadi Supervisors and Anganwadi 
Workers (AWWs) to ensure uniform implementation of the curricula, provision of Aadharshila 
(3–6 years) and Navchetana  (0–3 years) curriculum packages, facilitator handbooks, activity 
based learning materials, and implementation guidelines to frontline functionaries and age 
appropriate Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) practices through the Aadharshila 
and Navchetana curricula. Aadharshila and Navachetana curricula are implementing from June 
2025 in all AWCs of Andhra Pradesh.

GOVERNMENT OF INDIA 
MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS 
DEPARTMENT OF FERTILIZERS 
 
LOK SABHA 
 
UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 3380 TO BE ANSWERED ON: 07.08.2026 
 
Shortage of Urea and DAP 
 
3380. Shri Suresh Kumar Shetkar: 
 
Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
 
(a) whether the Government has identified the regions where Urea and DAP 
shortages were reported in the country during the last three years, if so, the details 
thereof and remedial action taken thereon, State/district-wise; 
 
(b) whether the Government has strengthened enforcement mechanisms against 
diversion, illegal sale and misuse of subsidized Urea and DAP fertilizers, if so, the 
details of cases registered and action taken thereon; 
 
(c) whether the Government proposes to provide additional financial assistance or 
special measures for small and marginal farmers affected by increasing fertilizer 
costs, if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor; 
 
(d) whether the Government has reviewed the fertilizer import policy, long-term 
supply agreements and domestic manufacturing plans to ensure uninterrupted 
availability of DAP and other essential fertilizers, if so, the details thereof; and 
 
(e) whether the Government has prepared a long-term fertilizer security roadmap for 
covering Urea and DAP production, import management, subsidy reforms and 
affordable availability for farmers, if so, the details thereof? 
 
ANSWER 
 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS & FERTILIZERS 
 
(SMT. ANUPRIYA PATEL) 
  
(a) Before the commencement of each cropping season, Department of Agriculture 
and Farmers Welfare (DA&FW), in consultation with all the State Governments, 
assesses the State-wise & month-wise requirement of fertilizers. On the basis of 
requirement projected by DA&FW, Department of Fertilizers (DoF) allocates adequate 
quantities of fertilizers to States by issuing monthly supply plan and continuously 
monitors the availability. 
 

 
Further, the distribution of fertilizers within the State at district/block level is done by 
the respective State Government. 
 
Accordingly, the availability of Urea and DAP has remained adequate across the 
States during the last three years. The State-wise information regarding the 
requirement, availability and sales of said fertilizers during the said period is placed 
at Annexure-A. 
 
(b) Fertilizers are declared as an essential commodity under the Essential 
Commodities Act, 1955 and notified under Fertilizer Control Order, 1985. State 
Governments are empowered to take action against persons involved in diversion, 
illegal sale and misuse of fertilizers, as per provisions of EC Act. Any complaint 
received at Department of Fertilizers level regarding such malpractices is sent to 
concerned State Government to take appropriate action under Essential Commodities 
Act, 1955 and Fertilizer Control Order, 1985.  
 
Further, Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare (DA&FW) in consultation 
with the State Governments is regularly monitoring the enforcement action taken by 
State Governments against the cases of black-marketing, diversion, hoarding and 
other malpractices on weekly basis. 
 
Accordingly, information received from the DA&FW regarding the action taken by the 
State Governments to check diversion and other malpractices during the ongoing 
Kharif 2026 season, for the period from April 2026 to July 2026 (till 31.07.2026), is 
placed at Annexure-B. 
 
(c) to (e) Under the Urea Subsidy Scheme, Urea is provided to the farmers at a 
statutorily notified Maximum Retail Price (MRP). The MRP of 45 kg bag of Urea is 
Rs. 242 per bag (exclusive of charges towards neem coating and taxes as 
applicable). The difference between the delivered cost of Urea at farm gate and net 
market realization by the Urea units is given as subsidy to the Urea 
manufacturer/importer by the Government of India. Accordingly, all farmers are being 
supplied Urea at the subsidized rate. 
 
Further, the Government had announced New Investment Policy (NIP) – 2012 on 2nd 
January, 2013 and its amendment on 7thOctober, 2014 to facilitate fresh investment 
in the urea sector and to make India self-sufficient in the urea sector. Total 6 new 
urea units have been set up under NIP-2012 which includes 4 urea units set up 
through Joint Venture Companies (JVC) of nominated PSUs and 2 urea units set up 
by the private companies. The units set up through JVC are Ramagundam urea unit 
of Ramagundam Fertilizers and Chemicals Ltd (RFCL) in Telangana and 3 urea units 
namely Gorakhpur, Sindri and Barauni of Hindustan Urvarak & Rasayan Limited 
(HURL) in Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand and Bihar, respectively. The units set up by 
private companies are Panagarh urea unit of Matix Fertilizers and Chemicals Ltd. 
(Matix) in West Bengal; and Gadepan-III urea unit of Chambal Fertilizers and 
Chemicals Ltd. (CFCL) in Rajasthan. Each of these units has installed capacity of 
12.7 Lakh

entries.head:
1 
 
GOVERNMENT OF INDIA 
MINISTRY OF AYUSH 
 
LOK  SABHA 
UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 3381 
ANSWERED ON 07.08.2026 
 
PROTECTION OF RIGHTS OF TRIBAL GROUPS IN TAMIL NADU  
3381. SHRI MANI A 
Will the Minister of AYUSH be pleased to state:- 
 
(a) whether the Government has undertaken any measures to protect the rights and ensure 
equitable benefit-sharing of local communities, traditional healers and tribal groups in Tamil 
Nadu who possess traditional knowledge relating to Ayurveda and medicinal herbs, particularly 
in districts such as Dharmapuri and if so, the details thereof; 
 
(b) the details of the mechanisms in place to regulate benefit -sharing arrangements between 
AYUSH manufacturing companies, herbal traders and such knowledge holders, including 
safeguards against unauthorised commercial exploitation;  
 
(c) whether any financial assistance, royalties, capacity -building programmes or community 
development initiatives have been extended to eligible communities in Tamil Nadu during the 
last five years, district-wise and if so, the details thereof; and 
 
(d) the further steps proposed to be taken by the Government to strengthen transparency, legal 
protection and fair compensation for traditional knowledge holders in the State? 
 
 
ANSWER 
THE MINISTER OF STATE (IC) OF MINISTRY OF AYUSH 
(SHRI PRATAPRAO JADHA V) 
 
(a) to (d)Ministry of Ayush is implementing Centrally Sponsored Scheme of National Ayush 
Mission (NAM) through State/ UT Government for overall development and promotion of 
Ayush systems across the country through States/ UTs including Tamil Nadu. Under NAM, 
Ministry of Ayush supports the efforts of State/ UT Government by providing financial 
assistance to them under different activities as per the provision of NAM guidelines against 
their submitted State Annual Plans (SAAPs). Public Health being State subj ect, improvement 
of infrastructure, training and capacity building for Ayush professionals comes under purview 
of respective State Government. However, the Research Council (s) of Ministry of Ayush 
namely Central Council for Research in Ayurvedic Sciences (CCRAS)  provides Ayurveda 
healthcare services in tribal areas across the country through the Tribal Health Care Research 
Programme (THCRP) under the Tribal Sub Plan (TSP), implemented through 14 CCRAS 
institutes in 14 States, including the Dr Achanta Lakshmipathi Regional Ayurveda Research 
Institute (ALRARI), Chennai and Captain Srinivasa Murthy Central Ayurveda Research 
Institute (CSMCARI), Chennai in Tamil Nadu.  The primary o bjective of the programme is to 

2 
 
provide Ayurveda healthcare services directly to tribal communities.  The Council also 
documents prevalent Local Health Traditions (LHTs), Ethno -Medicinal Practices (EMPs), and 
folklore claims among tribal populations.  
Moreover, Siddha Medicinal Plants Garden & Research Centre (SMPG&RC) , Salem, Tamil 
Nadu functioning under Central Council for Research in Siddha (CCRS) also conducts Health 
Camps through Swasthya Rakshan Programme for the tribal hamlets of Palamalai Hills for 5 
years. CCRS has taken initiatives to promote , validate and ensure Knowledge sharing through 
IMR projects for documenting folklore knowledge & traditional practitioners like “Survey on 
the traditional and common uses of medicinal plants from Dharmapuri District, Tamil Nadu”  - 
The Dharmapuri District of Tamil Nadu, India, has a diverse range of tribal communities. The 
study was designed in Dharmapuri District to document the existing medico -ethnobotanical 
knowledge among the three tribal communities, the Malayali, Irula, and Kurumba, in the 
treatment of a wide range of common ailments.  Siddha Medicinal Plants Garden ( SMPG), 
Mettur Dam functioning under CCRS organised Awareness program for the Government Tribal 
Residential Schools (Elementary and High School), Ramanpatti, Palamalai, Tamil Nadu during 
2024. Siddha Regional Research Institute ( SRRI), Puducherry organised Tribal Ayush 
Awareness health camp at Jally home, Puducherry during 2025.  Efforts have been made for 
screening and conducting research to manage anemia, malnutrition in tribal region with Siddha 
intervention and Siddha Aahaar. Health camp for screening anemia has been conducted during 
June 2026 at Tribal hamlet of Kalrayan Hills, Salem, Tamil Nadu through CCRS.

3384. SHRI PRADEEP PUROHIT:

(a) the details of programmes being implemented by the Union Government under the
National Health Mission (NHM) in Odisha during the last two years, indicating the objectives
and the funds released by the Central Government, year-wise and scheme-wise;
(b) the number of beneficiaries covered under various NHM schemes during the last two
years in the State, district-wise, particularly in Bargarh and Jharsuguda, scheme-wise and
year-wise;
(c) the details of financial assistance sanctioned, released and utilised under NHM for Odisha
during the last two financial years, indicating the Central and State shares separately; and
(d) whether the Government has assessed the adequacy of NHM infrastructure, healthcare
manpower and service delivery in Bargarh and Jharsuguda districts and if so, the details
thereof, along with any proposals under consideration for strengthening healthcare facilities
in these districts?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF STATEIN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND
FAMILYWELFARE
(SHRI PRATAPRAOJADHA V)
(a) to (d): ‘Public Health and Hospital’ is a state subject. The primary responsibility for
strengthening public healthcare system, including infrastructure, healthcare mapower and
service delivery lies with the respective State/Union Territories (UTs), including Odisha.
However, under National Health Mission (NHM), Ministry of Health and Family
Welfare provides technical and financial support to the States/UTs, including Odisha, to
strengthen the public healthcare system based on the proposals received in the form of

Programme Implementation Plans (PIPs). The Government of India provides approval for the
proposal in the form of Record of Proceedings (RoPs) as per norms & available resources.
The RoPs of the State of Odisha can be accessed at
https://nhm.gov.in/index4.php?lang=1&level=0&linkid=45&lid=58
Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (AAMs) represent one of the most significant
transformations in primary healthcare, serving as the cornerstone of universal health coverage
in India. Going beyond basic curative care, these centres offer an expanded package of
services, including screening and management of non-communicable diseases, maternal and
child health, mental health, oral health, eye care, ENT care, and palliative care. By shifting
the focus from curative care to community-based preventive and promotive health,
Ayushman Arogya Mandirs are laying the foundation for a healthier and more resilient India.
The details of central release under the National Health Mission (NHM) during last
two financial years from FY 2024-25 and 2025-26 to the State of Odisha is as follows:
(Rs. In Crore)
Financial Year Central Release Expenditure
2024-25 1,916.79 3,585.01
2025-26 1,760.71 4,330.21
Note: The above releases relate to Central Govt. Grants & do not include State share contribution.
The State/Union Territories (UTs)-wise details of healthcare facilities in the country,
including districts Bargarh and Jharsuguda of Odisha, can be accessed at the following link of
Health Dynamics of India (HDI), 2023-24:
https://www.mohfw-dohfw.gov.in/static/uploads/2026/05/57202cf30629539e4d0fb0a2f700ac62.pdf
To improve health infrastructure and services in public health facilities, government
has laid down Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS). They provide guidance on the health
system components such as infrastructure, human resource, drugs, diagnostics, equipment,
quality, and governance requirements for delivering health services at these facilities. They
are used as the reference point for public health care infrastructure planning and up-gradation
in the States and UTs. The Ministry has developed an open-source toolkit and a web-based
dashboard (www.iphs.mohfw.gov.in) launched under IPHS on 28th June 2024 to facilitate

self- assessment by all levels of facilities including Ayushman Arogya Mandirs. The IPHS
Dashboard is designed to monitor public health facilities' compliance with the IPHS 2022
standards and offers real-time updates, enabling oversight and data-driven decision-making to
identify gaps and facilitate timely interventions.
Under NHM, the performance of various health programmes including NHM
infrastructure, healthcare manpower and service delivery is regularly monitored in all the
States/UTs, through review meetings, mid-term reviews of key deliverables, field visits of
senior officials, promoting performance by setting up benchmarks for service delivery &
rewarding achievements etc. Also, Common Review Missions (CRM) are conducted annually
to assess and monitor the progress and implementation status under the scheme.

MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS 
DEPARTMENT OF FERTILIZERS 
 
LOK SABHA 
 
UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 3389 TO BE ANSWERED ON: 07.08.2026 
 
Demand and Supply of Fertilizers 
 
3389.  Shri Vijayakumar Alias Vijay Vasanth: 
Shri K Gopinath: 
 
Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
 
(a) whether the Government has made any assessment regarding the availability, 
demand, actual consumption and supply gap of Urea and DAP fertilizers in the 
country during the last three years and the current year, if so, the details of production 
and import, State-wise and year-wise; 
 
(b) whether farmers have faced shortages, delayed supply and increased prices of 
said fertilizers during peak sowing seasons, if so, the details thereof and the reasons 
therefor along wtih the steps taken to ensure adequate availability of fertilizers; 
 
(c) whether the Government has received complaints regarding non-availability, black 
marketing, hoarding or sale of said fertilizers at higher than prescribed rates, if so, 
the details thereof along with the action taken thereon and the distribution mechanism 
in place; and 
 
(d) whether the Government has made any assessment regarding the impact of rising 
international fertilizer prices and import dependency on the availability and cost of 
DAP in the country, if so, the details of initiatives, subsidies provided along with, the 
corrective measures taken to promote balanced and efficient use of fertilizers? 
 
ANSWER 
 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS & FERTILIZERS 
 
(SMT. ANUPRIYA PATEL) 
 
(a) to (d) To ensure adequate availability of fertilizers and prevent any shortage 
during each cropping season, the Government undertakes the following measures 
across the country: 
I. Before the commencement of each cropping season, Department of Agriculture 
and Farmers Welfare (DA&FW), in consultation with all the State Governments, 
assesses the State-wise & month-wise requirement of fertilizers. On the basis of 
requirement projected by DA&FW, Department of Fertilizers (DoF) allocates adequate 
quantities of fertilizers to States by issuing monthly supply plan and continuously 
monitors the availability. 

 
II. The movement of all major subsidized fertilizers is monitored throughout the 
country by an on-line web-based monitoring system called integrated Fertilizer 
Management System (iFMS). 
III. The gap between demand (requirement) and production for Urea & other 
fertilizer is met through imports. The import for the season is also finalized well in 
advance to ensure timely availability.  
IV. The State Governments are regularly advised to coordinate with manufacturers 
and importers for streamlining the supplies through timely placement of indents. 
V. Regularly coordination is done with the Ministry of Railways for giving sufficient 
rakes, priority to fertilizers and for timely evacuation of rakes for States. 
VI. The distribution of fertilizers within the State at district level is done by the 
concerned State government. 
Accordingly, the availability of Urea and DAP has remained adequate during the last 
three years and ongoing Kharif 2026 season. The State-wise information regarding 
the requirement, availability and sales of said fertilizers during the last three years 
and ongoing Kharif 2026 season is placed at Annexure-A. 
Further, under Urea Subsidy Scheme, Urea is provided to the farmers at a statutorily 
notified Maximum Retail Price (MRP). The MRP of 45 kg bag of Urea is Rs.242 per 
bag (exclusive of charges towards neem coating and taxes as applicable). The 
difference between the delivered cost of Urea at farm gate and net market realization 
by the Urea units is given as subsidy to the Urea manufacturer/importer by the 
Government of India. Accordingly, all Farmers are being supplied Urea at the 
subsidized rates. 
Besides, the Government has implemented Nutrient Based Subsidy (NBS) Scheme 
w.e.f. 01.04.2010 for Phosphatic and Potassic (P&K) Fertilizers. Under NBS Scheme, 
MRP of of P&K fertilizers are decontrolled and companies are free to fix MRP as per 
their business dynamics at a reasonable level. The NBS subsidy is provided 
manufacturer/importer on notified P&K fertilizers on its PoS sale during the season, 
depending on their nutrient content to ensure availability of fertilizers to farmers. The 
volatility in international prices of key fertilizers and raw materials is considered while 
fixing NBS rates for P&K fertilizers so that fertilizers remain affordable to the farmers. 
However, to make DAP being a key fertilizer, available at affordable price of Rs. 1350 
per 50 kg bag, special provisions like Rs. 3500 per MT to cover 'Other Costs' which 
includes costs incurred from factory gate to farm gate, advantage /disadvantage due 
to increase / decrease in international prices, provision for GST component included 
in the MRP and provision for reasonable return @ 4% of net MRP (MRP-GST) h

RISING CAESAREAN DELIVERIES
3390. DR. BACHHA VSHOBHA DINESH:
Will the MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE be pleased to state:
(a) whether the Government has taken cognisance of the consistently high and rising rates of
caesarean section deliveries in private healthcare institutions, significantly exceeding the
benchmark recommended by the World Health Organization;
(b) if so, the details of caesarean and normal deliveries reported during the last five years
with specific reference to Maharashtra;
(c) whether the Government has undertaken any assessment of non-clinical factors
contributing to this trend including institutional practices, financial incentives, medico-legal
considerations and socio-cultural preferences influencing the elective caesarean procedures
across the country, if so, the details thereof, State/UT-wise, and
(d) the regulatory, monitoring and corrective measures taken/proposed to be taken by the
Government to discourage unnecessary caesarean deliveries and safeguard maternal and
neonatal health outcomes?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF STATEIN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTHAND FAMILY
WELFARE
(SMT. ANUPRIYAPATEL)
(a) & (b) The rate of caesarean section deliveries in private healthcare institutions and the
details of caesarean section and total institutional deliveries reported over the last five years
for Maharashtra, are placed at the Annexure.
(c) As per the report of Population Research Centre (PRC) -JSS Institute of Economic
Research Dharwad, Karnataka, under Ministry of Health & Family Welfare (MoHFW),
Government of India, a study conducted on “Understanding the Context of Caesarean
Delivery from the Providers’ and Receivers’ Perspectives’’, mentions the main reasons behind
the increase rate of C-section Deliveries in the country as;
 Clinical Decision-Making by Doctor: Clinical indications, such as maternal age,
multiple pregnancies, fetal distress, previous C-sections, prolonged labour, placenta
previa, as well as maternal complications have a greater likelihood of caesarean
delivery.

 Patient/Community Preferences: These have decision-making role in the matter.
(d) Under the National Health Mission (NHM), various measures/initiatives have been taken
to discourage unnecessary caesarean deliveries across all States/UTs. The key measures are:
 CGHS empaneled hospitals are required to prominently display information regarding
the ratio of deliveries by Caesarean section vis-à-vis normal deliveries.
 Data Reporting and monitoring has been strengthened at health care facilities.
 Under National Quality Assurance Standards (NQAS), a dedicated C-section audit
component is embedded in the assessment checklist for Maternity OTs for all
Government Hospitals.
 Various training programs, including Daksh, Dakshta, Skilled Birth Attendant (SBA)
and Nurse Practitioner Midwifery (NPM) have been instituted to ensure the
availability of well-trained human resources, especially in remote areas in order to
promote normal deliveries.
To improve the maternal and neonatal health outcomes, the Government of India has taken
following initiatives under NHM:
 Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) is a demand promotion and conditional cash transfer
scheme for promoting institutional delivery.
 Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK) under which every pregnant woman
and sick infant is entitled to free delivery, including caesarean section, in public health
institutions along with provision of free transport, diagnostics, medicines, blood, other
consumables & diet.
 Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan (PMSMA) provides pregnant
women a fixed day, free of cost assured and quality antenatal check up by a
Specialist/Medical Officer on the 9th day of every month.
Extended PMSMA (e-PMSMA) strategy was launched for individual tracking of
high-risk pregnant women till a safe delivery.
 LaQshya improves the quality of care in labour room and maternity operation
theatres to ensure that pregnant women receive respectful and quality care during
delivery and immediate post-partum.
 Surakshit Matritva Aashwasan (SUMAN) aims to provide assured, dignified,
respectful and quality healthcare at no cost and zero tolerance for denial of services
for every woman and newborn visiting the public health facility to end all preventable
maternal and newborn deaths.
 Optimizing Postnatal Care aims to strengthen the quality of postnatal care by laying
emphasis on detection of danger signs in mothers and incentivizing Accredited Social
Health Activists (ASHAs) for prompt detection, referral & treatment of such high-risk
postpartum mothers.
 Monthly Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Day is an outreach activity at
Anganwadi centers for provision of maternal and childcare including nutrition in
convergence with the Integrated Child Development Scheme (ICDS).

MEASURES TO REDUCE C-SECTION DELIVERY RATES
†3391. SHRI BHAUSAHEB RAJARAM WAKCHAURE:
Will the MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE be pleased to state:
(a) whether the Government is aware of the scientific research and outcomes of 10,000
successful deliveries using the ‘Evidence-based Upright Indian Birthing Positions’ developed
by Dr. Prabodh Joshi from the Shirdi Parliamentary Constituency in Ahilyanagar District of
Maharashtra, if so, the details thereof;
(b) whether this research has proven effective in reducing cesarean (C-section) delivery rates
and improving maternal and child health outcomes, if so, the details thereof;
(c) whether the Government plans to replicate and implement this model across Primary
Health Centres (PHCs) in rural areas of the country;
(d) whether financial assistance is likely to be provided for training and the publication of
literature to disseminate this research and if so, the details thereof; and
(e) whether the Government proposes to integrate this methodology into the national policy
for ‘Safe Motherhood’ Surakshit Matritva and if so, the details thereof?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF STATEIN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY
WELFARE
(SMT. ANUPRIYAPATEL)
(a) to (e) As per the information received from the state of Maharashtra, the District
Health administration, Ahilyanagar has not received any official information regarding the
development of evidence-based upright Indian birthing positions by a practicing doctor in
Shirdi parliamentary constituency. The District Health administration has not conducted or
received any evaluation report assessing the reduction in c-section delivery rates or
improvement in maternal and neonatal health outcomes.
However, the Government of India has already circulated the “Guidelines on
Operationalization of Midwifery Units” to all States/UTs, for the establishment of Midwifery-
Led Care Units (MLCUs). These units promote physiological childbirth by offering women a
choice of scientifically validated, evidence-based alternative birthing positions and are
expected to contribute towards reducing unnecessary caesarean sections.
Further, under the National Health Mission (NHM), financial support is being provided to
States/UTs for the establishment and operationalization of such Midwifery-Led Care Units,

entries.t: Establishment of Additional Cancer Hospital in Assam
entries.head:
GOVERNMENT OF INDIA
MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE
DEPARTMENTOF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE
LOK SABHA
UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 3392
TO BE ANSWERED ON 7TH AUGUST, 2026
ESTABLISHMENT OF ADDITIONAL CANCER HOSPITALIN ASSAM
3392. MD. RAKIBUL HUSSAIN:
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE be pleased to state:
(a) whether the Government proposes to establish additional cancer hospitals and advanced
oncology centres in Assam, if so, the details thereof;
(b) the present availability of radiotherapy, chemotherapy and cancer diagnostic facilities in
Government hospitals of the said State;
(c) whether patients from Dhubri and adjoining districts continue to travel long distances for
treatment, if so, the details thereof; and
(d) the steps taken by the Government to ensure affordable and timely cancer care?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF STATEIN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND
FAMILYWELFARE
(SHRI PRATAPRAOJADHA V)
(a) to (d) The Department of Health and Family Welfare provides technical and financial support
to States and Union Territories across the country under the National Programme for Prevention
and Control of Non Communicable Diseases (NP-NCD) as part of the National Health Mission
(NHM). The programme focuses on strengthening infrastructure, human resource development,
screening, early diagnosis, referral, treatment, and health promotion for NCDs. Under NP-NCD,
770 District NCD Clinics, 233 Cardiac Care Units and 6,410 NCD clinics at Community Health
Centres were set up across the country. In addition, 524 Day Care Cancer Centres (DCCCs) are
functional across the country to ensure cancer care accessibility at district hospital level, out of
which 06 DCCCs are functional in the state of Assam.
Further, the Department of Health and Family Welfare is implementing ‘Strengthening of
Tertiary Care Cancer Facilities’ Scheme under the National Programme for Prevention and
Control of Non-Communicable Diseases. Under the Scheme, support is provided to States and
Union Territories for setting up of State Cancer Institutes (SCIs) and Tertiary Care Cancer
Centres (TCCCs) in Government Medical Colleges/Hospitals or Regional Cancer Centres. Till
date 39 institutions (19 SCI and 20 TCCC), including Gauhati Medical College & Hospital,
Guwahati, as a State Cancer Institute in Assam were approved across the country.

Treatment of major NCDs including Cancer treatment are available under Ayushman Bharat –
Pradhan Mantri Jan ArogyaYojana (AB PMJAY). This scheme provides for Rs. 5 lakh per family
annually for secondary and tertiary care hospitilization in the empanelled public and private
hospitals. The Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana (PMBJP) and Affordable
Medicines and Reliable Implants for Treatment (AMRIT) Pharmacies improve access to
affordable cancer medicines, stents, and implants, reducing out-of-pocket expenses and
supporting long-term treatment adherence.
Under NHM, National Free Drugs Initiative and Free Diagnostic Services ensure essential
medicines and diagnostics at public health facilities, reducing out-of-pocket expenses. Anti-
cancer drugs are included in the Essential Drugs List at District and Sub-Divisional Hospitals
under NP-NCD.

entries.head:
GOVERNMENT OF INDIA
MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE
DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE
LOK SABHA
UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 3394
TO BE ANSWERED ON 07TH AUGUST 2026
UG AND PG SEATS IN MEDICAL COLLEGE
3394. SHRI JANARDAN SINGH SIGRIWAL:
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE be pleased to state:
(a) whether the Government has taken steps to increase the number of medical colleges along
with Undergraduate (UG) and Postgraduate (PG) medical seats in the country during the last
five years;
(b) if so, the details thereof indicating the increase in the number of medical colleges and UG
and PG medical seats across the country, year-wise and State/UT-wise;
(c) the number of new medical colleges established or approved and the increase in UG and
PG medical seats in Bihar during the last five years, year-wise; and
(d) whether the Government has any proposal to further increase the number of medical
colleges along with UG and PG medical seats in Bihar and if so, the details thereof,
locationwise, along with the timeline for its implementation?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF STATEIN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY
WELFARE
(SMT. ANUPRIYAPATEL)
(a) to (d): The Government has significantly increased the number of medical colleges and,
consequently, the number of MBBS and PG seats in the country. The number of medical
colleges has increased by 118.6%, from 387 before 2014 to 846 at present. Further, the
number of MBBS seats has increased by 172.4%, from 51,348 before 2014 to 1,39,864 at
present. Similarly, the number of PG seats has increased by 176.9%, from 31,185 before 2014
to 86,360 at present. In Bihar, the number of medical colleges has increased by 35%, from 20
to 27, while the number of MBBS seats has increased by 77.4%, from 2,415 to 4,285 during
the last five years.
The measures/steps taken by the Government to augment the medical education
facilities and to improve the medical standards in the country include: -

i. Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) for establishment of new medical colleges by
upgrading district/ referral hospital under which 157 new medical colleges have been
approved including 08 colleges in Bihar.
ii. CSS for strengthening/ upgradation of existing State Government/ Central
Government medical colleges to increase the number of MBBS (UG) and PG seats,
under which support has been provided for increase of 4977 MBBS seats in 83
colleges with an approved cost of Rs. 5972.20 Cr, 4058 PG seats in phase-I in 72
colleges with an approved cost of Rs. 1498.43 cr and 4000 PG seats in phase-II in 65
colleges with an approved cost of Rs. 4478.25 Cr.
iii. Also, Cabinet approved Phase-III of (CSS) for “Strengthening and upgradation of
existing State Government/Central Government Medical Colleges/Standalone PG
Institutes/Government Hospitals” to facilitate increase of 5000 PG seats with an
enhanced cost ceiling of Rs. 1.5 Crore per seats and extension of existing CSS for
UG Scheme for 5023 MBBS seats with a enhanced cost of Rs. 1.5 Crore per seats.
The timeline for implementation of both the Scheme is 2028-2029.
iv. Under “Upgradation of Government medical colleges by construction of Super
Specialty Blocks” component of Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana
(PMSSY), a total of 75 projects have been approved, of which 71 projects are
complete.
v. Under the Central Sector Scheme for setting up of new AIIMS, 22 AIIMS have been
approved. Undergraduate courses have started in 19 of these.

†3395. DR. ANAND KUMAR:
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE be pleased to state:
(a) whether the Government is aware that more than 80 unregistered nursing homes, hospitals and
pathology laboratories were sealed and notices were issued to several other institutions for violating
regulatory norms during a recent drive in the border districts of Uttar Pradesh, including Bahraich,
adjoining the Indo-Nepal border;
(b) if so, the details thereof;
(c) the details of inspections conducted, unregistered health institutions identified, notices issued,
institutions sealed and the legal action taken against them during the last three years, State/UT-wise;
(d) whether the Government has assessed the effectiveness of the registration and inspection
mechanism for private health institutions in border and rural areas, if so, the details thereof; and
(e) the steps being taken by the Government to further strengthen the regulatory mechanism to
ensure quality and safe healthcare services in the country?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF STATEIN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY
WELFARE
(SHRI PRATAPRAOJADHA V)
(a) to (c): ‘Public Health’ and ‘Hospital’ are State subjects, the primary responsibility for planning,
implementing, maintaining and to set up adequate number of healthcare facilities as per requirement
is of that State Government. Under the National Health Mission, financial and technical support is
provided to States/UTs to strengthen their healthcare system.
As per the information provided from State Government of Uttar Pradesh, 7 hospitals were
deregistered, FIRs were lodged in 8 cases, 11 hospitals were sealed, and notices were issued to 97
hospitals. In addition, 7 laboratories/diagnostic centres were sealed and notices were issued to 24
laboratories/diagnostic centres.
(d): As informed by the State Government of Uttar Pradesh, registration of clinical establishments
is carried out through the Janhit Swasthya Portal. Applications are processed by the concerned
district authorities, and the Chief Medical Officers undertake verification/inspection, as applicable,
before approval of registration in accordance with the prescribed regulatory framework. The online
mechanism also facilitates systematic processing and monitoring of applications.

(e): As reported by the State, the Government of Uttar Pradesh is also taking steps to further
strengthen the regulatory framework including appropriate provisions relating to the Clinical
Establishments Act/Rules and clearly defined Minimum Standards, with the objective of
strengthening registration, regulation, monitoring quality assurance and patient safety in clinical
establishments.
Further, the implementation progress and performance of schemes under National Health
Mission (NHM) are regularly monitored through regular review meetings and field visits conducted
through Common Review Mission (CRM). Also, periodic assessments e.g. National Family Health
Survey, Sample Registration System are used to gauge health indicators and implementation status.

AWHs in Andhra Pradesh?

(a) to (e) Anganwadi Workers (AWWs) and Anganwadi Helpers (AWHs) are honorary

services in the area of child care and development to help the local community, for which the y 
are paid honorarium. This honorarium is increased from time to time. From 1 st October, 2018, 
Government of India has enhanced the honorarium of AWWs at Anganwadi centres (AWCs) 
from Rs.3,000/- to Rs.4,500/- per month and AWHs from Rs.1,500/ - to Rs.2,250/- per month 
as per the defined cost sharing ratio between the Centre and States and UTs. In addition, States 
and UTs are also paying additional monetary incentives and top ups to these functionaries from 
their own resources which vary from State to State. Details of additional top ups provided by 
States and UTs are at Annexure.  
Besides, performance linked incentive of Rs.500/ - per month is provided to AWWs and 
Rs.250/- per month to AWHs. 

Under Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0, AWWs have been technologically 
empowered with the provision of smartphones for efficient monitoring and delivery of services. 
Poshan Tracker which is a mobile phone application that has digitized physical reg isters used 
by Anganwadi workers. This improves the quality of their work while simultaneously enabling 
them for real-time monitoring of all activities going on in the Anganwadis.   
To incentivize and encourage the AWWs and AWHs, various initiatives have been undertaken 
including the following: 
(i)  Promotion: Under Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0, promotional opportunities 
for AWWs and AWHs have been enhanced. 50% posts of AWWs are to be filled by AWHs 
with 5 years of experience and 50% posts of Supervisors are to be filled by promotion  of 
AWWs with 5 years of experience subject to fulfilment of other criteria.  
(ii)  Leave: 20 days’ annual leave and paid maternity absence of 180 days and paid absence on 
abortion/ miscarriage once for 45 days.  
(iii) State Governments and UT Administrations have been requested to encourage eligible 
AWWs and AWHs to get themselves enrolled under the Pradhan Mantri Shram Yogi Mandhan 
(PM-SYM) Pension Scheme, which is a voluntary and contributory pension scheme for the 
unorganized sector in the country to ensure old age protection.  
(iv)  Social Security Insurance Schemes: Insurance benefits have been provided to AWWs and 
AWHs under Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana (PMJJBY) for life cover worth Rs.2.00 
lakh (covers life risk, death due to any reason) in the age group of 18 to 5 0 years and under 
Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana for accidental cover of Rs.2.00 Lakh (accidental death 
and permanent full disability) /Rs.1.00 Lakh (partial but permanent disability) in the age group 
of 18-59 years. 
(v)     Retirement date: States and UTs have been requested to adopt a uniform retirement date 
i.e 30th April of each year with respect to AWWs and AWHs to ensure proper human resource 
planning. 
(vi)   Annual Healthcare coverage of Rs. 5 Lakhs under Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan 
Arogya Yojana (AB-PMJAY) to all AWWs and AWHs in pursuance to budget announcement

Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0 is a Centrally Sponsored scheme. The Central

engagement/ video conferences are held with all States and UTs regularly to monitor the

entries.t: Stunting, Wasting and Anaemia among Children
entries.head:
GOVERNMENT OF INDIA  
MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT  
 
LOK SABHA  
UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 3398  
ANSWERED ON 07.08.2026  
  
STUNTING, WASTING AND ANAEMIA AMONG CHILDREN  
 
3398. SMT. APARAJITA SARANGI:  
 Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a)  whether the Government has evaluated the progress of Mission Saksham Anganwadi 
& POSHAN 2.0 in reducing child stunting, wasting and anaemia, if so, the details 
thereof; 
(b)  the details of the children identified as malnourished and treated during the last three 
years, State/UT-wise including Odisha; and  
(c)  the details of the corrective measures proposed for high -burden districts? 
  
  
ANSWER 
 
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT  
(SHRIMATI SAVITRI THAKUR)  
  
(a) to (c): An outcome-based evaluation study of Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0 
was conducted by Development Monitoring and Evaluation Office  (DMEO), NITI Aayog in 
2025 in 12 States and one Union Territory. Evidence from institutional assessments and 
household surveys indicated that in its current form, Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 
2.0 (Mission Poshan 2.0) represents the Government’s latest effort to holistically combat 
malnutrition and promote child development, by building on past programs with a co nverged 
and strengthened approach. Also, a third -party evaluation and impact assessment of Poshan 
Abhiyaan, the predecessor programme to Mission Poshan 2.0, was conducted by NITI Aayog 
in 2020. It found the relevance of Poshan Abhiyaan to be satisfactory f or tackling malnutrition 
in the country. 
Ministry of Women and Child Development (MoWCD) under Mission Poshan 2.0 has rolled 
out the Poshan Tracker as an ICT -based tool for continuous monitoring of beneficiaries 
registered at Anganwadi Centres (AWCs). The application facilitates dynamic identific ation 
and monitoring of malnutrition indicators such as stunting, wasting, and underweight 
prevalence among children. The State -wise and year -wise information on nutrition indicators 

among children under 5 years is available at Poshan Tracker public dashboard at the given link: 
https://www.poshantracker.in/statistics.  
As informed by the State Government of Odisha, the recovery rate among discharged SAM 
children improved steadily from 54% in 2023 to 79% in 2024 and 82% in 2025. As of 5 August 
2026, the cumulative recovery rate further increased to 83%, with 1,01,469 of t he 1,22,789 
discharged children reported as cured, indicating sustained improvement in treatment outcomes 
under Purna Aahara. 
The State of Odisha has adopted a continuum of nutrition -specific and nutrition -sensitive 
interventions, with intensified identification, treatment and follow -up of children at risk. The 
following measures are prioritised in high -burden districts: 
• Early identification and active case tracking: Strengthen regular growth monitoring at 
AWCs and conduct focused drives such as Ojan Utsav. Utilising Poshan Tracker for 
beneficiary registration, portability, monitoring and timely follow -up. 
• Intensified treatment through Purna Aahara: Ensure uninterrupted provision of 
augmented energy -dense Take-Home Ration (THR) and one egg to SAM children for 
112 days (16 weeks), supported by fortnightly counselling and growth monitoring. 
Review every non-responsive case individually. 
• Clinical referral and protocol-based care: Refer children with medical complications to 
NRCs or health facilities for specialised management. Provision of medicines, 
deworming and other treatment as per the approved protocol, with post -discharge 
follow-up. 
• Enhanced nutrition support for MAM and SUW children: Provision of age -specific 
additional support under SNP and MSPY, including Chhatua, premixes, eggs, bananas 
or seasonal fruits, and hot cooked meals to address acute and chronic dietary gaps.  
• Last-mile coverage in hard-to-reach habitations: Expansion of effective implementation 
of Pada Pusti Karyakram by decentralising spot feeding in remote hamlets and tagged 
villages, including morning snacks and hot cooked meals for preschool children.  
• Family counselling and behaviour change: Use home visits, recipe demonstrations, 
community events, Poshan Maah and Poshan Pakhwada to reinforce breastfeeding, 
appropriate complementary feeding, dietary diversity, hygiene and timely care-seeking. 
• POSHAN Abhibhabaks: Senior district -level officers are assigned as POSHAN 
Abhibhabaks to monitor high -burden Anganwadi Centres, identify implementation 
gaps and facilitate timely corrective action.  
  
• District Nodal Officer Monitoring: Department has assigned senior officers as nodal 
officer for each district who are regularly touring and monitoring the nutritional 
interventions in field. 

• Technology-enabled THR Quality Assurance: Department is ensuring quality of THR 
through use of computer vision cameras installed in various THR producing units.

pendency levels of FTSCs;

disposal rates and reduce pendency in FTSCs;

(a) to (c):  A Centrally Sponsored Scheme to set up Fast Track Special Courts (FTSCs), including 
exclusive POCSO (ePOCSO) courts was launched in October 2019, for the expeditious trial and 
disposal of pending cases related to rape and offences under the Protection of C hildren from Sexual

Law & Justice has written to Hon’ble Chief Ministers and Chief Justices of the High Courts regarding 
need for timely action and strict compliance with timelines under the POCSO Act and Bharatiya 
Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. In addition, the performance of FTSCs is a regular agenda item in 
the Inter -State Zonal Council meet ings to improve inter -governmental coordination and expedite 
justice delivery.

including 399 exclusive POCSO (e -POCSO) Courts, were functional in 29 States/UTs. Since the

UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 3400
TO BE ANSWERED ON 7TH AUGUST, 2026
MANAGEMENT OF NON-COMMUNICABLE DISEASES
3400. SHRI B Y RAGHA VENDRA:
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE be pleased to state:
(a) the major policy initiatives undertaken by the Government during the last decade to
strengthen the prevention, early detection and management of Non-communicable diseases
(NCDs), particularly diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, cancers, chronic respiratory
diseases, year-wise;
(b) the details of population-based screening programmes undertaken by the Government for
major NCDs during the last ten years, indicating the cumulative number of individuals screened
for diabetes, hypertension and common cancers, along with the role of Ayushman Arogya
Mandirs in expanding such screening services;
(c) the measures taken by the Government to strengthen the continuum of care for NCD patients
through digital health initiatives, including patient registries, telemedicine, follow-up
mechanisms and other technology-enabled interventions;
(d) the progress achieved in strengthening NCD services including dedicated clinics, diagnostic
facilities, trained healthcare personnel and their integration with primary healthcare; and
(e) the future roadmap of the Government for strengthening the prevention, early detection and
management of NCDs?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF STATEIN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND
FAMILYWELFARE
(SHRI PRATAPRAOJADHA V)
(a) & (b) Public Health and Hospitals are state subject. The Department of Health and Family
Welfare provides technical and financial support to States and Union Territories across the
country under the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Non Communicable
Diseases (NP-NCD) as part of the National Health Mission (NHM). The programme focuses on
strengthening infrastructure, human resource development, screening, early diagnosis, referral,
treatment, and health promotion for NCDs.
Under NP-NCD, the Government of India focuses mainly on Diabetes, Hypertension, common
cancers (Oral, Breast and Cervical), Chronic Kidney Disease, ST-segment Elevation Myocardial
Infarction (STEMI), Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease, Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver
Disease (NAFLD) and Stroke.

Under NP-NCD, individuals of 30 years and above are screened for common NCDs including
three common cancers (oral, breast and cervical cancer), Diabetes and Hypertension through
various health facilities. Prevention, control & screening services are provided through trained
frontline workers. The progress achieved in terms of population screening is attached at
Annexure-I.
(c) The Government has undertaken several digital initiatives under the NP-NCD and the
Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) to strengthen the continuum of care for NCD patients.
The NP-NCD Portal supports management of NCD services, including beneficiary registration,
risk assessment, population-based screening, diagnosis, treatment, follow-up and programme
monitoring. Teleconsultation services are provided through the eSanjeevani platform to improve
access to specialist care, particularly in remote and underserved areas. Further, real-time
dashboards and digital analytics facilitate monitoring of programme performance, while line lists
generated through the portal support timely follow-up of patients by ASHAs and other frontline
healthcare workers, thereby improving treatment adherence and continuity of care.
(d) & (e) Under NP-NCD, 770 District NCD Clinics, 233 Cardiac Care Units and 6,410 NCD
clinics at Community Health Centres were set up across the country. In addition, 524 Day Care
Cancer Centres (DCCCs) are functional across the country to ensure cancer care accessibility at
district hospital level. Further NP-NCD gives financial support under NHM for awareness
generation (IEC) activities.
Under the Strengthening of Tertiary Care Cancer Facilities Scheme, the Government has
approved 19 State Cancer Institutes (SCIs) and 20 Tertiary Cancer Care Centers (TCCCs) to
strengthen tertiary-level cancer care across the country.
To strengthen comprehensive cancer care, an integrated referral network between DCCCs and
State SCIs/ TCCCs was setup. Under this hub-and-spoke model, SCIs/ TCCCs provide
specialized cancer treatment, while DCCCs deliver chemotherapy, follow-up, supportive and
palliative care closer to patients’ homes.

(a) whether the Government has reviewed Tele Mental Health Assistance and Networking
Across States (TELE-MANAS) and mental-health access and sanctioned capacity,
services, beneficiaries, claims or staffing, as applicable, if so, the details thereof;
(b)the details of funds, posts, facilities, utilisation and outcomes during the last three years,

Health Assistance and Networking Across States (Tele-MANAS) in terms of its reach and
user engagement across the country. A Rapid Assessment Report on Tele MANAS (2024)
was published by WHO, which provides an overview of programme performance, reach,
